analysis.one_liner: Extends the federal ban on military-style semiautomatic rifles and large-capacity magazines for ten more years.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee or floor vote, and the existing 1994 assault weapons ban expired on schedule in September 2004.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1994, Congress banned the manufacture and private sale of certain semiautomatic assault-style weapons and large-capacity ammunition magazines, but wrote the law to repeal itself after ten years. This bill would have extended that ban for another decade, to 2014. Instead, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of communities affected by gun violence and police officers, according to the bill's bipartisan supporters, who argued that keeping combat-style rifles and high-capacity magazines off the civilian market would reduce casualties in mass shootings and street violence.

how_it_helps.text: The bill extends the 1994 ban, which prohibited the manufacture and private sale of 19 named semiautomatic firearms and copies with certain combat features, for an additional ten years, to September 13, 2014.
The existing ban was written to repeal itself on September 13, 2004 unless Congress acted, so this bill was the vehicle for keeping it in force.
The ban restricted large-capacity ammunition magazines, which supporters link to higher death tolls in mass shootings.

analysis.who_pays: Firearms manufacturers and dealers, who would have remained barred from making and selling the listed semiautomatic rifles and large-capacity magazines to the public, and gun buyers who wanted those specific weapons.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and some buyers

drawbacks.text: Opponents argued the 1994 ban keyed on cosmetic features rather than how guns function, so functionally similar firearms remained legal and the law covered only a narrow list of weapons.

An honest supporter had to acknowledge that government-funded studies of the ban's first decade found its measurable effect on gun crime was modest, largely because it grandfathered millions of existing weapons and covered a limited set of guns; supporters argued the effect would grow as pre-ban weapons aged out.
The ban imposed real costs on a lawful industry and on gun owners who would have continued to face criminal penalties for making or buying the covered weapons and magazines.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stakes were asymmetric but the evidence was genuinely contested: the ban covered a narrow, feature-based list of guns and grandfathered existing ones, so its proven crime effect over 1994-2004 was modest. Supporters argued renewal was a low-cost, proven-in-place restriction on the weapons most associated with mass-shooting casualties; opponents argued it restricted lawful commerce without proven benefit. Either way, the bill never received the hearing or vote that would have tested those arguments.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on February 24, 2004 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and no senator ever got to vote on it before Congress ended on January 3, 2005; by then the 1994 ban had already lapsed on its own sunset date in September 2004.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 24, 2004 by Senator Dianne Feinstein with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors including Republicans John Warner, Mike DeWine, and Lincoln Chafee.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, the only committee action ever taken on it.
No hearing, committee markup, or floor vote is recorded in the bill's complete action history before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
The 1994 law the bill would have extended was set to repeal itself on September 13, 2004, so without congressional action the ban expired that September.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers and sellers came out ahead: when Congress let the ban lapse without a vote, they regained the ability to make and sell the prohibited semiautomatic rifles and large-capacity magazines to the public. Because no renewal reached the floor, the president never had to take a position on signing it.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend the assault weapons ban and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. John Warner
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, giving the renewal bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled floor time or a vote on the reauthorization, despite the president saying he would sign an extension if it passed.

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or committee vote on the bill after it was referred to his committee.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against extending the ban and against lawmakers who supported it, and supported alternatives that would have weakened the ban's scope.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Said he would sign an extension if Congress passed it, but did not lobby Congress to bring it to a vote, and it never reached his desk.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship (13 cosponsors: 9 Democrats, 3 Republicans, 1 Independent), but the Republican leadership that controlled the Senate calendar never allowed it a vote.

industries.note: The 1994 ban barred them from making the listed combat-style semiautomatic rifles and large-capacity magazines for the civilian market, and its expiration in September 2004 restored that product line and revenue. The industry's gain from the bill's death was the public's continued exposure to those weapons.
Renewal would have kept the banned rifles and high-capacity magazines off their shelves; letting the ban lapse reopened a sales category for them.
